entries.title: Ukraine airstrike on bus in Russian-occupied Luhansk kills 9
entries.summary: Russian authorities in the occupied territory say the drone attack caused injuries. Kyiv also destroyed another Wildberries warehouse.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine airstrike on bus in Russian-occupied Luhansk kills 9

August 26, 2026

Russian authorities in the occupied territory say the drone attack caused injuries. Kyiv also destroyed another Wildberries warehouse.

A Ukrainian airstrike killed nine people in Ukraine's eastern, Russian-occupied Luhansk region on Wednesday, according to Leonid Pasechnik, leader of Russia's occupying forces there.

Pasechnik labeled the strike "a war crime," saying it had killed eight people on the spot and that another person, a 20-year-old woman, died of her injuries shortly thereafter.

The bus was said to have been carrying 15 people, with five more reported injured.

Ukraine keeps up strikes in Russia, destroys another major warehouse

With US-brokered peace talks failing to get off the ground and the Kremlin sticking to its maximalist demands before agreeing to end its four-and-a-half-year invasion, Kyiv and Moscow have continued to escalate their air campaigns.

Kyiv again targeted logistics infrastructure on Wednesday, using drones to destroy another Wildberries warehouse, this one in Russia's Tambov region, southeast of Moscow.

Tambov's governor said the 100,000 square-meter (1.1 million square-foot) facility — an area roughly the size of 14 soccer fields — had been "completely destroyed by fire."

Wildberries is Russia's biggest online retailer.

Ukrainian strikes on its facilities not only disrupt the Kremlin's military logistics — Kyiv says Wildberries aids the military war effort — they also strike at Russia's civilian economy and thus touch everyday Russians.

This week, Kyiv expanded its target list to include Russia's number two online retailer, Ozon.

In an analysis of satellite imagery, Reuters news agency estimated that at least 1.9 ​million square meters of warehouse space had been severely damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks on more than 20 Wildberries and Ozon facilities in recent weeks.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: No, this wasn't a "completely normal summer", despite far-right climate denial
entries.summary: Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.

As a summer of European extreme heat draws to a close, politicians are looking back at the toll. Germany recordedaround 14,000 heat-related deaths, almost two-thirds in one scorching week of June alone.  A Dutch bank estimated summer heat will cost the EU €180 billion in lost GDP. And in June, European farmers lostapproximately 9 million tons in grain crops. 

Climate change, long a politically charged topic, has become a daily reality for people around the world. These effects and more are making it increasingly difficult to challenge what people are seeing with their own eyes.

Yet that hasn’t stopped the global populist right from trying. Richard Tice, deputy leader of the UK’s far-right Reform Party said"climate change has always happened, it always will," adding that it was arrogant to try to stop it. He encouraged the British public to enjoy the heat.  

In the US, Harriet Hageman, a Republican politician and potentially Wyoming’s next senator, told far-right channel Real America’s Voice that Europe’s heatwave was business as usual. "It's called summer. Some years are hotter than others and some years are colder than others," she said. "But that's just the cyclical nature of weather."

And Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of Germany’s far-right AfD party tolda journalist in recent days that it’s been a "completely normal summer." He dismissed climate change as "hype." 

 

But claims like these don’t stand up to scientific scrutiny.  

As NASA statesplainly: "Scientific evidence continues to show that human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth’s surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth’s climate."

This was not 'a completely normal summer'

This summer has been historically hot. Independent climate monitoring bodies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration(NOAA) in the US, the Copernicus Climate Change Service in the European Union and the Japan Meterological Agency, all called last month either the joint-warmest or joint-second warmest month on record.  

The conditions have led energy plants to halt production, outdated concrete motorways blowing up, and older buildings overheating during the day and barely cooling down at night — threatening inhabitants with exposure to heat stress.

The extreme heat was felt almost everywhere on the globe. According to NOAA’s data, it was the warmest July ever for North America, Africa and Asia.

The continental United States just surpassedits warmest July records. They were previously set in 1936, during the infamous Dust Bowl that scorched the US Great Plains with extreme temperatures, and in 2012, when North America suffered an extreme heatwave.  

And the daily average sea surface temperature hitits highest level since records began in 1979 — reaching 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) this month. That’s a result of both human-driven warming as well as El Nino, a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures.  

How climate change supercharged this summer's fires

In Spain, the far-right Vox party saidfires — which burned more than 254,000 hectares of land across the country this season — were not connected to climate change. 

Yet experts agree rising global temperatures played a major role in the intense wildfire season that also scorched large parts of France and Canada. That’s because extreme heat creates ideal conditions for wildfires to start and spread.

A field of climate research called attribution science explores the extent to which climate change exacerbates extreme weather events like this summer’s wildfires. Using models, researchers compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world in which there is no human-caused warming.

Analyses done this summer showthat hotter global temperatures created conditions that made the wildfires in Spain 20 times more likely to happen, and twice as probable in France.  

This is due to a phenomenon known as weather whiplash, where ecosystems swing dramatically between wet and dry conditions.

When the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, rainfall is intensified, and plants grow. Then, in summer, that same warm atmosphere draws water from soil and plants, worsening drought and drying out vegetation, turning it into the perfect fuel for fires.

"We know — and this is mathematically proven — that the probability of having fire weather that can sustain and create this kind of event has been altered by climate change," Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, told DW about this summer’s fires in Spain and France.

Climate change’s ripple effects

Overall, this summer has left its mark in numerous ways that are impossible to ignore.

Bodies of water across Europe are drying out under the intense heat. Parts of the Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, making it impossible for ships to pass through in some spots.  

This has a number of knock-on effects. Drinking water costs could rise dramatically as much of Germany’s clean water first passes through reed-filled riverbanks that are crucial for filtration.

Supply chains are also be disrupted, as vessels can’t carry as much cargo when water levels are lower, increasing prices across the economy in products like steel or petroleum.

In America, drought conditions are wreaking havoc on crops and livestock. In June, the US Department of Agriculture said the 10-month stretch from August 2025 to May 2026 was the nation’s driest period since 1976-77. 

Now, 59% of the country’s sorghum is being grown in  areas experiencing drought. More than half the nation's cattle production and almost two-thirds of spring wheat production is happening under water scarcity.

Such conditions can put direct strain on the country's food supply, increase prices and threaten rural livelihoods.

By any measurement — thermometers, drought maps, or death tolls — and in much of the world, this summer has been historically extreme.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Tim Curry, of 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dies at 80
entries.summary: The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and William Shakespeare.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and William Shakespeare.

Actor Tim Curry died at the age of 80, Variety, TMZ and other celebrity news outlets reported on Wednesday.

A cause of death was not immediately given but Curry had been in poor health for some time following a severe stroke that left him confined to a wheelchair and wrote in his memoir "Vagabond" last year that he was still not able to walk.

Curry won Laurence Olivier and Tony Award nominations for his work on stage in the UK and the US, as well delivering Emmy-winning TV performances later in his career.

Who was Tim Curry?

Curry was born in Cheshire into a Navy family in 1946 and spent his life bouncing around an array of different homes in the UK and even Hong Kong. He ultimately went to school in Bath, impressing as a soprano singer, and university in Birmingham.

He played in London musicals in the late 60s and early 70s seeking his big break, which came in a 1973 unusual musical ultimately destined to graduate to the silver screen.

Curry was given the role of the lingerie-clad sweet singing transvestite Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" in 1975. Despite the very German sounding name and initial rehearsals with a German and American accent, he ultimately played the mad scientist with an exaggerated upper class Belgravia accent, in what a Guardian newspaper 1973 review referred to as a "garishly Bowiesque performance as the ambisextrous doctor."

He went on to play an array of other roles that involved elaborate costumes, unusual mannerisms, and often a fairly pronounced dark but also comedic side in his career.

These included Gomez Addams in the "Addams Family Reunion" cinema reboot, Long John Silver in "Muppet Treasure Island," the suspicious Plaza Hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Pennywise the Clown in a miniseries based on Stephen King's novel "It," and even as the voice of Chancellor Palpatine in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars."

In another Star Wars connection, Curry was even cast as the Joke for "Batman: The Animated Series," having been considered for the role in the 1989 film as well, until Mark Hamill supplanted him.

Curry also played some of history's most consequential figures like Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, William Shakespeare, and even King Arthur — albeit in the Monty Python musical stage show "Spamalot." He was also among the first actors to branch out into video game roles, perhaps most notably as the fictional Soviet military officer Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3.

He released several solo studio albums and also contributed to various soundtrack records throughout his career, with his musical background apparent in many of his acting roles.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
entries.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.

Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.

It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.

So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?

Debut with a bang

Caroline Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, from 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.

The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.

What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations: It includes references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," says Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick tells DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."

Polarizing ambition

The success led to the media becoming interested in the young author, and quickly showed that Caroline Wahl does not care much for conventions: She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper last weekend. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me (...). Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind: "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."     

A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, she said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, she faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."

Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asks literary scholar Matthias Schaffrick: "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, she also taps into the role of an influencer, says Matthias Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself admits that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."

'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to best‑sellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers come to different conclusions on whether Caroline Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."

Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, on this year's longlist, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" (The Assistant) has not been included. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? (...) The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."

Presumably, Caroline Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.

entries.title: Saxony-Anhalt: an AfD stronghold in Germany's east
entries.summary: Saxony-Anhalt is a structurally weak, predominantly rural state. Could it become the first German state to be governed by the far-right AfD?
entries.content:
Germany

Saxony-Anhalt: an AfD stronghold in Germany's east

August 26, 2026

Saxony-Anhalt is a structurally weak, predominantly rural state. Could it become the first German state to be governed by the far-right AfD?

Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage: Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still provides around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the River Elbe, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.

Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, in September 2026, international attention is likely to turn to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, holds a clear lead in all opinion polls.

The AfD is far ahead in the polls

Just before the election, the AfD is polling at more than 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since its re-establishment in 1990, trails far behind, with support ranging between 23% and 26%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution classifies the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. The Left Party is polling at 13%, while support for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stands at between 6% and 7%. It remains uncertain whether the Greens and the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP) will succeed in returning to the state parliament.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as State Premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said that he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Haseloff's successor, Sven Schulze, also of the CDU, must now take on the AfD. If he fails, the CDU's long dominance of state politics could come to an end in September. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the FDP.

1994 experiment: a minority government backed by the PDS

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt once again found itself at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the late Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party (SED).

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.

Dissatisfaction, demography and immigration

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in Saxony-Anhalt feel with developments in Germany. In the years following reunification, large numbers of jobs disappeared, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the Statistical Office of Saxony-Anhalt, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.

A long history of far-right support

According to many observers, the DVU's success some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy programme.

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded. "I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely." In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script."

One thing seems certain: on September 6, all eyes will be on this small state in the center of Germany.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Frankfurt Airport worker dies after malaria infection
entries.summary: An unusual cluster of malaria cases at Frankfurt Airport infected six employees, one fatally. It is thought to have been caused by a mosquito brought in on an aircraft.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

An unusual cluster of malaria cases at Frankfurt Airport infected six employees, one fatally. It is thought to have been caused by a mosquito brought in on an aircraft.

At least one Frankfurt Airport employee has died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by an infected mosquito brought into Germany on an aircraft.

Germany's DPA news agency reported that another airport employee had died of malaria in July, citing Frankfurt's health authorities. At the time, the cause of death was not immediately clear.

The case is part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country.

What we know about the Frankfurt Airport malaria death

Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport confirmed the latest death on Wednesday. A spokesperson said the company had been informed by the responsible health authority and expressed "deepest sympathy" to the employee's relatives.

In total, six airport employees are known to have contracted so-called airport malaria in connection with their work.

The first four infections became known in mid-July. Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI) for public health said those affected fell ill between July 4 and 6 and that the infections were believed to have been transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by aircraft.

What is airport malaria?

Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad.

Airport malaria, however, can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area.

The RKI describes such cases as very rare. The last documented case at Frankfurt Airport was in 2023.

Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual.

The remaining infected employees are receiving medical treatment, while the local health authority continues to monitor the situation.

Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin.

Fraport has also informed employees at the airport and advised them to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Meta settles in US states lawsuit on teen user addiction
entries.summary: Meta has agreed to pay what could amount to billions of dollars and to implement platform usage limitations on young users in a lawsuit brought by US states. The challenge revolved around addiction issues and overuse.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

Meta has agreed to pay what could amount to billions of dollars and to implement platform usage limitations on young users in a lawsuit brought by US states. The challenge revolved around addiction issues and overuse.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to pay as much as $16.7 billion (roughly €14.3 billion) and to impose new limits on how teenagers use its social media sites as part of a lawsuit in California brought by a number of US states. 

The settlement still requires court approval.

The proposal was filed in federal court on Wednesday and seeks to resolve claims from a coalition of 47 US states in total.

As well as the financial damages, it foresees Meta introducing various limitations and changes designed to improve child safety and discourage or prevent overuse and social media activity overnight or during school hours.

What did officials say about the settlement?

"Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement as the settlement was announced.

He called the agreement "real change, real transparency, and real enforceable protections for children."

The filing states that the agreement does not amount to any admission of liability or wrongdoing from Meta, which had consistently denied the allegations.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones, however, argued that Meta had intentionally put young people's health at risk and that the changes helped to stop this.

"For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health," Jones said, arguing that the settlement "will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm." 

What changes does the settlement require of Meta?

Meta is proposing a series of usage limitations for people under the age of 18, including a "hard cap" on the daily total time spent on their sites.

The cumulative all-day cap is to be set at 2 hours of daily use across Meta's various platforms. Parents will be authorized to lift the restriction. Meta said that in cases where it detects distinct users with multiple accounts, it would apply across them.

Beween midnight and 6 a.m., underage users will also be suspended from the sites.

In what Meta calls "School Mode," notifications will be muted by default between 8 a.m and 3 p.m., with teens no longer receiving push notifications during these hours, "except for direct messages and alerts about their account safety or security."

The minimum age to open accounts on Facebook and Instagram in most US states is 13 (or higher in a few instances) so in theory for younger children there should be no issue. California's attorney general said Meta would be required to institute additional measures designed to identify and remove younger users of its platforms.

California's attorney general also said Meta would also be required to respond to 90% of teen reports on potentially harmful content within 6 hours. It said that Meta would be required to offer under-18s the option of a non-personalized feed as their default.

What did Meta say about the settlement, and its call to YouTube and TikTok to join in?

Meta noted that Wednesday's agreement was reached with both Republican and Democrat attorneys general and said the plan built "on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens."

The company said it wanted to ensure that teens benefit from "this new industry standard," but said "we cannot do it alone." 

"These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place," the company said.

Meta said that the payments would be distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period, also issuing a slightly higher potential maximum total figure of $18 billion.

It said that participating states would receive "approximately 70%" of the allocated payment over the decade. The remaining roughly 30%, it said, would be released only after two specific conditions were met.

Meta said it required that "YouTube and TikTok implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode, and age assurance figure," as well as the two companies each paying an amount matching its 30% figure.

If industry peers also sign up, Meta said, then it would beef up its own restrictions, "reducing the Daily Limit to one hour per app and expanding Night Mode hours" to 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., rather than the initial midnight to 6 a.m..

"Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution," Meta's Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said. "We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away."

Mahoney said that "as a parent" he was "proud" of Meta's efforts in the past to safeguard young users and of Wednesday's "new groundbreaking agreement."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Reports: UEFA backs off FIFA boycott threat
entries.summary: UEFA is reportedly set to withdraw a threat to boycott FIFA tournaments over a plan to partially privatize football tournaments. The Under-20 Women's World Cup is to be hosted by Poland next month.
entries.content:
August 26, 2026

UEFA is reportedly set to withdraw a threat to boycott FIFA tournaments over a plan to partially privatize football tournaments. The Under-20 Women's World Cup is to be hosted by Poland next month.

English newspapers The Times, the Guardian and news agency Reuters reported on Wednesday that UEFA, football's European governing body, was set to drop its threat to boycott all FIFA tournaments.

The decision to allow European teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland came after UEFA had reportedly received guarantees that football's world governing body would not revive a plan to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments to private investors. FIFA President Gianni Infantino had dropped his plan to create a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE) in the face of widespread protest last month.

UEFA spearheaded opposition to the plan but it had also demanded that "assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," something that until now, FIFA had declined to do. The reports suggest this demand has now been met.

The reports also said UEFA would use a meeting of its executive committee and most of the presidents of its 55 national associations in Monaco on Thursday to inform them that the U20 tournament could go ahead.

'Not a UEFA defeat'

The Guardian reported that the FIFA and UEFA officials had been in private talks for weeks with the aim of preventing a boycott.

"It's not a UEFA defeat, rather the reality of avoiding hurting young players during a once in a lifetime ⁠opportunity," a source familiar with the discussions told Reuters. "The actions and insistence on change will ​continue."

The Times reported that UEFA was working on other ways to try to step up the pressure on Infantino.

It cited a letter reading that "UEFA hereby gives formal notice that it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters.

"You and FIFA are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or FIFA's possession, custody, or control."

'Best possible conditions' for the tournament

Prior to the latest reports, the Polish FA (PZPN) told DW in a statement that it was continuing with preparations to host the Under-20 Women's World Cup as planned.

"Our priority remains to ensure the best possible conditions for the competition and for all participating teams," the statement read.

"For many of these young players, this tournament represents an important milestone in their sporting careers, and we remain fully focused on delivering an event worthy of their talent and commitment."

The tournament kicks off with the opening match between Poland and Argentina in Katowice on September 5.

Gianni Infantino is expected to stand for re-election at a FIFA Congress next March and so far no other candidate has come forward to challenge him. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin has already said he will not run.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: Could Syria become the focus of an Israeli-Turkish conflict?
entries.summary: An Israeli attack on a Syrian military airfield just recently demonstrated once again that Syria is becoming a key battleground for the rivalry between regional powers. At the forefront: Israel and Turkey.
entries.content:
Syria

Could Syria become the focus of an Israeli-Turkish conflict?

August 26, 2026

An Israeli attack on a Syrian military airfield just recently demonstrated once again that Syria is becoming a key battleground for the rivalry between regional powers. At the forefront: Israel and Turkey.

Following US mediation, Syrian and Israeli representatives met in Jordan last weekend for the first time in months. The talks aimed to defuse tensions following the recent Israeli attacks on Syrian territory and prevent hostilities between Israel and Turkey from spilling over into Syria.

The escalation was sparked by an Israeli attack on the Abu Duhur military airfield in Idlib Province on August 18. According to Syrian sources, the attack struck the runway and storage facilities without causing any fatalities. Israel stated that Syria had violated — or threatened to violate — a previous security agreement by allowing Turkish troops to use the airfield. Damascus and Ankara rejected these allegations.

 The US criticized the attack by its Israeli ally as an "unnecessary escalation." In diplomatic terms, this amounts to a fairly clear show of rhetorical support for Ankara and Damascus.

Israel views a potential Turkish military presence in Syria as a red line. Yet, it remains unclear whether such a deployment is planned in the long term or whether it was even imminent at the time of the attack. Evidence on this matter is not publicly available.

However, as early as April 2025, Reuters news agency cited anonymous sources saying Turkey had inspected at least three air bases in Syria where it might want to station troops as part of a planned joint defense pact. Israeli airstrikes were already taking place at that time as well.

The Washington-based think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), which is considered pro-Israel, justifies the attack as follows: "Israel worries that Ankara could eventually use its military presence in Syria as a platform to pressure or threaten Israel, and remains wary of the close relationship between Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa and the Turkish leadership."

Syria, Turkey and Israel disagree on the future order

For Bente Scheller, Syria expert at the German Green Party-affiliated Heinrich Böll Foundation, this explanation falls short.

"There is no evidence so far that Turkish troops are actually supposed to be stationed there," she told DW. While Israel may indeed have its own intelligence, the recent attack must be viewed against the backdrop of Israel's overall policy toward Syria as well as Turkey's growing regional role, she noted.

Marcus Schneider, a Middle East analyst at Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation — which is affiliated with the German Social Democratic Party (SPD) — in Beirut, also points out that a struggle for power and influence is unfolding in Syria and beyond.

"The attack primarily raises the question of what kind of military order will emerge in Syria in the future," he told DW. In his view, Israel wants to keep Syria weak, as a sovereign state that controls its own airspace would restrict Israel's military freedom of action. "The corridor for attacks against Iran runs through Syria," explained Schneider. A sovereign Syria could therefore pose a strategic obstacle to Israel.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, Israel's heightened security concerns are understandable, adds Scheller. In addition, Israel is certainly viewing with concern another development that extends beyond Syria.

"Israel is undoubtedly aware of how Turkey is currently attempting to position itself as a regional hegemon," Scheller said. The attack on Abu al-Duhur is therefore "clearly also a message to Turkey."

Turkey supports Syrian President al-Sharaa and is committed to a unified Syria which includes the territory in the country's northeast, where the majority of Syria's Kurdish population is located. For years, Turkey has been attacking the former Kurdish-led autonomous zone along its southern border. On Tuesday, the commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced the official dissolution of the group.

An analysis by the US think tank Carnegie Foundation describes the situation as a strategic rivalry between Israel and Turkey: "The northeast is also the main arena where two externally-driven strategic visions for Syria collide." The International Crisis Group also views Syria as a fault line between Turkey, a rising regional power, and Israel.

Syria's closer relations with the US

Syria's improved relations with the US — which amount to US support — offer new prospects for the country, despite the Islamist past of its new leader, President Ahmad al-Sharaa. In summer 2025, the US began gradually easing sanctions, and in November of that year, al-Sharaa was received by US President Trump at the White House. The two met again on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara in July 2026. In early 2026, the US withdrew its military forces from Syria, and on Monday (August 24), it officially removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

However, under the current circumstances, Syria appears to be relying primarily on itself, including in its relations with Turkey. For analyst Marcus Schneider, however, a potential Turkish presence is not comparable to the former Iranian presence during the Assad regime.

Contrary to the view held in Israel, he argues that Ankara is primarily interested in a stable Syria and in securing its southern border. "The idea that Turkey, a NATO member, would attack Israel, a nuclear power, is preposterous," he said. The real problem, he argues, is that Israel increasingly views Turkey as a strategic adversary and interprets Turkey's capabilities as evidence of hostile intentions.

Al-Sharaa is seeking foreign policy support wherever he can find it, observes Scheller. "In recent months, Turkey has increasingly become one of the countries from which Damascus expects concrete assistance." This is not just a matter of security: Ankara wants to expand its regional influence and, at the same time, has an interest in maintaining stability along the shared border, she said.

Who will ultimately determine Syria's security order?

Following the overthrow of Syria's longtime ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, Israel established a security zone north of the Golan Heights and has repeatedly attacked Syrian targets. According to an analysis by the Carnegie Foundation, the calls for such a buffer zone is deeply rooted in Israeli security thinking; less clear, however, is the intention — sometimes attributed to Israel by analysts — of permanently fragmenting Syria to keep it weak.

The US think tank FDD takes a different view, pointing to Israel's skepticism toward the new Syrian military and Turkish support. However, Schneider notes that the new regime in Syria has extended a hand to Israel from the outset, despite its ideological origins. "Damascus does not want a war with Israel," he said, adding that it wants to regain its national sovereignty. It is precisely this aspiration that clashes with Israel's military presence and its red lines.

Syria needs a viable political order

"Syria is caught between two militarily powerful neighbors that respect neither its sovereignty nor its territorial integrity," said Scheller.

In her view, the outcome will now depend on al-Sharaa's negotiating skills. "How can he defend Syrian sovereignty against these two neighbors and actually chart a distinct Syrian path?" However, Syria's weakness does not lie solely in its military inferiority. The country must first develop a viable political order, she notes.

This is also the starting point for political scientist Haid Haid in an analysisfor the British think tank Chatham House: "Syria's foreign policy success has been significant, but it cannot, on its own, secure stability. In this sense, Syria's greatest vulnerability lies not at its borders, but within."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy in Africa
entries.summary: Zambia's democratic institutions are under scrutiny, as the opposition continues to dispute the election results and courts remain closed. Weeks after the election, Zambia’s election story might be far from over.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy

August 26, 2026

Zambia's democratic institutions are under scrutiny, as the opposition continues to dispute the election results and courts remain closed. Weeks after the election, Zambia’s election story might be far from over.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema winner of the August 13 presidential election.

His closest challenger, Brian Mundubile, received 38% of the vote, according to official results published last week. However, Mundubile has since announced on several occasions that he would be challenging that result, and that his National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) "shall not relent" in the face of any obstacle.

That challenge, however, comes as Zambia's courts have all remained closed since August 24 until further notice, with officials citing "security concerns."

The timing of this closure has raised questions about opposition voices having access to judicial election safeguards during this crucial stage of the post-election process, as random reports of irregularities continue to surface.

Election dispute continues to unfold

The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has called for the urgent restoration of access to the courts and for alternative arrangements to be enacted for urgent cases.

LAZ President Arnold Kaluba said security measures must not undermine any access to justice or judicial independence.

"Such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a manner that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary," he stressed.

Meanwhile, the Human Rights Commission of Zambia has also expressed concern; its chairperson, Pamela Towela Sambo, warned that disruption to judicial operations could affect fundamental rights in the country, including access to a fair trial and legal remedies.

"[If] the right to a fair trial is delayed, there is increased risk of arbitrary detentions, while access to remedies is effectively blocked," she said.

'Irregular' submission of petition documents

However, the ongoing election dispute has taken a new turn: Zambia's Chief Justice Mumba Malila, acknowledged on August 25 that he had received documents described as a presidential election petition through his private email-address.

Malila described the method of submission as "highly irregular" —despite the current circumstances allowing no access to legal procedures. He said he nevertheless referred the documents to the Constitutional Court to determine whether this qualified as a petition having been formally filed.

The distinction here is important: The receipt of such documents does not confirm that a presidential election petition has been formally lodged per se.

The latest development comes as the courts remain closed, adding to questions about how election-related cases can be filed and processed.

Government continues to cite security concerns for court closure

Meanwhile, the presidency has rejected suggestions that the court closures were intended to prevent and intervene with any challenges to the election result.

Hichilema's chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the security measures were of a "intelligence-led and preventive" nature, adding that they involved several government institutions beyond courts, and that they were intended to protect officials, institutions and members of the public.

He also maintained that people with legitimate grievances remained free to pursue remedies provided by law.

But during the election itself, there had already been suspensions of voting at some ballot boxes amid reports of violence. Questions about the independence of the media had also surface in the run-up to the vote.

Concerns about access to justice and public confidence remain strong, especially against this backdrop; the Zambia Executive Director Maurice Nyambe of Transparency International said in this context the country needs stronger institutions for resolving political disputes.

"At this stage of the electoral process, Zambia does not need fewer avenues for resolving political disputes. It needs stronger, accessible, and trusted institutions through which those disputes can be peacefully resolved."

Political commentator and human rights activist Laura Miti meanwhile questioned the lack of a fuller public explanation for the closure, writing on Facebook that "if you are going to unprecedentedly close the courts, you owe the nation an explanation beyond a blanket — there is a security threat."

A test beyond the ballot box

Zambia has long been regarded as one of Southern Africa's more stable multiparty democracies with a reputation for political stability and peaceful transfers of power.

But the current dispute comes at a time when democratic institutions across the region keep facing growing scrutiny over contested elections and political transitions. Therefore, the handling of situation will likely be observed beyond Zambia and the southern African region.

For Zambians, the issue goes beyond the contest between Hichilema and Mundubile; it is about how political disagreements can be resolved peacefully through independent, accessible and trusted institutions.

That notion is perhaps best reflected on the streets of Lusaka; a citizen of the capital simply told DW: "We are anxious and afraid because we do not know the truth about what is happening."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson
